THE CORE IDEA

runs.text: Fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand through changes in government purchases, taxes, and their effects on consumption. Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left. After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect. A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

WATCH OUT

runs.text: A common mistake is to classify fiscal policy from the economy's condition rather than the government's action. Higher purchases or lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases or higher taxes are contractionary.

WORKED EXAMPLE: SHIFTING AGGREGATE DEMAND

runs.text: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level P. A horizontal line at price level P crosses three downward-sloping aggregate-demand curves. AD1 intersects at output Y1, AD2 lies to the right and intersects at Y2, and AD3 lies farther right and intersects at Y3, so Y1 is less than Y2, which is less than Y3.

runs.text: At the displayed price level P, an expansionary fiscal action shifts aggregate demand from AD1 to AD2. Real output demanded rises from Y1 to Y2 at that fixed price level. A larger action could shift demand to AD3 and quantity demanded to Y3, but the graph does not establish which package is desirable; that depends on the output gap and timing.
